title: NBA fines Clippers $30M, strips five first-round picks, suspends owner Ballmer one year for salary cap circumvention
dek: The NBA concluded a year-long investigation into the Clippers' salary cap circumvention scheme and issued historic penalties: a $30 million fine to the organization, suspension of owner Steve Ballmer for one year, forfeiture of five first-round draft picks spanning 2029-2033, and a $700,000 fine to Kawhi Leonard. The investigation found the team orchestrated fake endorsement deals to mask additional compensation to Leonard.
author: The GoCheckMySports Desk
key_fact: The Clippers will forfeit five consecutive first-round picks (2029-2033) and owner Steve Ballmer faces a one-year suspension, the most severe organizational penalty in NBA history for salary cap circumvention.
bottom_line: The Clippers will pursue legal remedies despite the NBA-NBPA agreement deeming penalties final and binding; the success or failure of any external appeal will set precedent for whether conferences and leagues can enforce competitive rules against determined institutional resistance. The question of whether Leonard's minimal penalty relative to leadership's suspension indicates investigative leverage or enforcement disparity may drive broader scrutiny of how the league handles future violations.
body:
The NBA concluded a year-long investigation into the Los Angeles Clippers' salary cap violations and imposed penalties on multiple levels of the organization: a $30 million fine to the team itself, a one-year suspension of owner Steve Ballmer, forfeiture of five consecutive first-round draft picks from 2029 through 2033, and a $700,000 fine to Kawhi Leonard, per CBS Sports and Yahoo Sports reporting.
According to CBS Sports, the scheme involved endorsement agreements with companies including Aspiration (which later declared bankruptcy with its founder sentenced to 14 years for investor fraud), Daktronics, Boingo Wireless, and Lockton Insurance.
The investigation determined, per CBS Sports, that the Clippers "affirmatively initiated off-court income opportunities" for Leonard with multiple companies and "induced" those companies into deals "by offering them business from the team." The team also broke league rules by "paying personal expenses on behalf of Leonard and his representatives" and "failing to report improper solicitations for off-court income opportunities" made through Leonard's then-business manager, Robertson. Leonard violated the circumvention rules "through the conduct of Robertson on his behalf," the NBA concluded according to CBS Sports reporting, finding that Leonard "pressured the Clippers to assist him in obtaining off-court income opportunities, successfully obtaining those opportunities, and failing to reimburse payments by the Clippers for personal expenses."
President of Business Operations Gillian Zucker was suspended without pay for one year, and President of Basketball Operations Lawrence Frank was suspended without pay for six months, per CBS Sports. The investigation traced the scheme's origins to September 2025, when investigative journalist Pablo Torre released a podcast alleging salary cap circumvention; , as filings showed Leonard listed as a creditor in the company's bankruptcy.
The Clippers and Leonard have publicly denied the allegations since they surfaced. The organization issued a statement characterizing the investigation as "heavily biased" and stating that "what the league told us privately differs from what it announced today publicly," according to CBS Sports. The Clippers said they "will now fight just as hard to demonstrate our innocence" and "intend to vigorously challenge these findings and penalties through every avenue available." In a letter to Silver, the team declared: "This investigation has been flawed from the outset" and called it "a witch hunt" that "flies in the face of fundamental fairness." Leonard, through a statement released by his new agent Harrison Gaines, said he accepts "full responsibility for lapses in judgment" by people in his "inner circle" but had "no knowledge of any intent on anyone's part to circumvent the salary cap." He stated he entered into agreements "in good faith, fully committed to fulfilling my obligations."
The NBA and Players Association agreed the penalties are "final and binding on all parties," though CBS Sports reports that according to analyst Marc Stein, there is no mechanism in NBA bylaws allowing the Clippers to appeal; any challenge would have to proceed through external legal channels. Leonard was not suspended from play or had his contract voided. He was traded to the Toronto Raptors in a deal agreed to in June but held pending the investigation's outcome; the Clippers received Brandon Ingram, Gradey Dick, two first-round picks, one pick swap, and two second-rounders, per CBS Sports. Commissioner Silver stated: "I am deeply disappointed by the flagrant violations of our rules and by the Clippers' institutional and leadership failures that led to this misconduct. The severity of the penalties reflects the seriousness of the violations."
